question: What is the difference between quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC)?
option_a: QA is the whole programme (responsibilities, standards, records, training); QC is the actual testing and monitoring of equipment
option_b: QC is the whole programme; QA is the individual tests
option_c: They mean exactly the same thing
option_d: QA is done by manufacturers; QC is done by patients
explanation: QA covers everything that assures quality, from purchase specifications to training and record keeping. QC is the set of practical tests within it, done daily, monthly, quarterly or annually, aiming at consistent performance and stability.
feedback_b: This is the wrong way round.
feedback_c: QC is one part of a QA programme.
feedback_d: Both are the responsibility of the department, with medical physics and the supplier.

question: According to the World Health Organization's definition, what is the aim of QA in diagnostic imaging?
option_a: Images that consistently give adequate diagnostic information at the lowest possible cost and patient exposure
option_b: The highest possible image quality whatever the dose
option_c: As many examinations as possible each day
option_d: Making sure every image looks identical
explanation: QA is an organised effort to keep images consistently good enough for diagnosis while keeping patient dose and cost as low as possible.
feedback_b: QA balances image quality against dose; the best possible image at any dose isn't the aim.
feedback_c: Throughput is not the aim of QA.
feedback_d: Images vary with the patient; QA aims for consistent diagnostic quality, not identical images.

question: What is acceptance testing?
option_a: Checking that new equipment meets its purchase specification and is safe before clinical use
option_b: The daily check radiographers do before the first patient
option_c: Repairing equipment after a fault
option_d: Testing equipment just before it is disposed of
explanation: Acceptance testing happens after installation and before clinical use. It confirms the equipment does what was specified and agreed with the supplier.
feedback_b: Daily checks are routine quality control.
feedback_c: After a repair, testing verifies the fault has been corrected.
feedback_d: Acceptance testing happens at the start of the equipment's life.

question: What is the main purpose of commissioning tests?
option_a: To record baseline performance values that later tests are compared with
option_b: To decide which equipment to buy
option_c: To train referrers
option_d: To set the patient dose limit
explanation: Commissioning measures how the equipment performs when it is working well. These baselines let routine tests detect any change in performance.
feedback_b: Purchase specifications come before the equipment arrives.
feedback_c: Training referrers isn't part of equipment testing.
feedback_d: Patients have no dose limits; DRLs are set separately.

question: Why are routine performance tests compared with the baseline values?
option_a: To detect gradual deterioration in performance before it affects patients
option_b: To prove the equipment is new
option_c: To work out each patient's dose
option_d: To replace the need for maintenance
explanation: Equipment drifts over time. Comparing with baseline values detects and diagnoses changes; after a repair, a further test verifies that the cause has been corrected.
feedback_b: Baselines track change over the equipment's life.
feedback_c: Patient doses are estimated from exposure factors, DAP and the EI.
feedback_d: Maintenance is needed throughout the QA cycle.

option_b: A list of national diagnostic reference levels
option_c: Guidance on referral criteria for doctors

question: A test result is beyond the remedial level but within the suspension level. What happens?
option_a: Remedial action is needed, but the equipment may stay in use meanwhile, based on a risk assessment and an agreed timescale
option_b: The equipment must be removed from clinical use immediately
option_c: No action is needed
option_d: The equipment must be replaced
explanation: At the remedial level, the risk of continued use is assessed, a timescale for the fix is agreed and any restrictions on use are followed.
feedback_b: That is what the suspension level recommends.
feedback_c: Exceeding the remedial level always needs action.
feedback_d: Remedial action usually means adjustment or repair, not replacement.

question: What does the suspension level recommend?
option_a: That the equipment is removed from clinical use immediately
option_b: That the equipment is used only for chest X-rays
option_c: That the test is repeated next year
option_d: That the radiographer increases the mAs to compensate
explanation: Performance beyond the suspension level is poor enough that continued use would be unsafe or give inadequate images.
feedback_b: Restricted use can follow a remedial-level result, not a suspension-level one.
feedback_c: Suspension means action now, not at the next routine test.
feedback_d: Changing exposure factors doesn't fix a faulty unit and may raise doses.

feedback_d: Many image quality tests are done by radiographers and medical physics.

option_a: They are part of the QA programme and may be needed as evidence for HSE inspectors
option_b: So the patient can see them

option_d: They don't need to be documented

question: What does the light beam alignment test check?
option_a: That the light field matches the X-ray field, so collimation shows the area actually irradiated
option_b: That the room lights are bright enough
option_c: That the tube output is consistent
option_d: That the focal spot is the right size
explanation: The edges of the light field are marked, an exposure is made and the two fields are compared. If they don't match, patients may be irradiated outside the intended area, or anatomy may be cut off.
feedback_b: It tests the collimator's light, not the room lighting.
feedback_c: Output is tested with an ionisation chamber.
feedback_d: Focal spot size is tested with a pinhole or star test object.

question: Which instrument is used to test tube output?
option_a: An ionisation chamber with an electrometer, at a known distance from the tube
option_b: A Geiger–Müller counter
option_c: A star test object
option_d: A lead bar pattern
explanation: The chamber measures dose for a range of exposures to find the output per mAs, how it varies with mA and kVp, whether repeated exposures are consistent, and whether it has changed from the baseline.
feedback_b: A GM counter detects radiation but doesn't measure dose accurately.
feedback_c: A star test object measures focal spot size.
feedback_d: A bar pattern measures spatial resolution.

question: How is the accuracy of the tube voltage checked?
option_a: With an electronic kVp meter, at a range of settings
option_b: By looking at how dark the image is
option_c: With a TLD worn by the radiographer
option_d: By timing the exposure with a stopwatch
explanation: A kVp meter measures the actual tube potential. The test checks it matches the selected value, doesn't change with mA or time, and stays steady during the exposure.
feedback_b: Image appearance depends on many factors and can't measure kVp.
feedback_c: A TLD records personal dose.
feedback_d: Exposure time doesn't tell you the voltage.

question: How is an automatic exposure control (AEC) tested?
option_a: By exposing Perspex or water phantoms of different thicknesses at different kVp, and checking the detector dose indicator stays consistent
option_b: By exposing a volunteer several times
option_c: By turning the AEC off and checking the image
option_d: By measuring the light field size
explanation: A working AEC should give a consistent dose to the detector over a wide range of patient thicknesses and tube voltages. The mAs and detector dose indicator are recorded for each exposure.
feedback_b: People are never exposed for testing; phantoms simulate patients.
feedback_c: Turning the AEC off doesn't test it.
feedback_d: Light field size is the light beam alignment test.

question: What does the guard timer do, and how is it tested?
option_a: It ends the exposure if the AEC fails to; it is tested by blocking the AEC chambers with lead
option_b: It times how long patients wait; it is tested with a clock
option_c: It limits the kVp; it is tested with a kVp meter
option_d: It controls the anode rotation; it is tested by listening
explanation: If the AEC chambers receive no radiation, the guard timer stops the exposure at a set limit, protecting the patient from a very large dose. Blocking the chambers with lead simulates this failure.
feedback_b: The guard timer is a safety feature of the exposure, not a waiting-time clock.
feedback_c: kVp isn't limited by the guard timer.
feedback_d: Anode rotation is separate from exposure termination.

question: Which test objects are used to measure the size of the focal spot?
option_a: A pinhole or a star test object
option_b: A Leeds test object
option_c: A Perspex block
option_d: An ionisation chamber
explanation: A pinhole smaller than the focal spot produces an image of it. A star test object of lead spokes blurs at the centre; the size of the blurred area gives the focal spot size.
feedback_b: Leeds test objects assess image quality, such as low-contrast detail.
feedback_c: Perspex blocks simulate patients for AEC testing.
feedback_d: An ionisation chamber measures dose.

question: What does a lead bar pattern test measure?
option_a: The limiting spatial resolution: the finest detail the system can show
option_b: The tube output
option_c: The kVp accuracy
option_d: The patient's dose
explanation: The bar pattern has groups of lead lines at increasing spatial frequency. The finest group that can still be seen as separate lines shows the limiting resolution.
feedback_b: Output is measured with an ionisation chamber.
feedback_c: kVp is measured with a kVp meter.
feedback_d: Bar patterns test the imaging system, not dose.

question: What is a Leeds test object used for in routine QC?
option_a: Checking the system can still show low-contrast detail
option_b: Measuring the focal spot
option_c: Testing the light beam alignment
option_d: Calibrating personal dosemeters
explanation: Leeds test objects contain details of decreasing contrast. Counting how many can be seen, and comparing with the baseline, shows whether low-contrast performance has deteriorated.
feedback_b: Focal spot size is measured with a pinhole or star test object.
feedback_c: Light beam alignment compares the light and X-ray fields.
feedback_d: Personal dosemeters are calibrated by the dosimetry service.

question: How is the uniformity of a digital detector tested?
option_a: An exposure is made with nothing in the field, and pixel values in each quadrant and the centre are compared
option_b: An image is taken with no exposure, to measure noise
option_c: A wire mesh is imaged to look for blurring
option_d: The detector is weighed
explanation: With no object in the beam, a uniform detector should give similar values across its area. Regions of interest in the four quadrants and the centre are compared.
feedback_b: That is the dark noise test.
feedback_c: That tests the uniformity of resolution, not of the detector's response.
feedback_d: Weight says nothing about the detector's performance.

question: Explain the difference between quality assurance and quality control, giving examples of each. (4 marks)
model_answer: Quality assurance is the whole programme for making sure images are consistently of diagnostic quality at the lowest reasonable dose and cost. It includes responsibilities, purchase specifications, image quality standards, monitoring and maintenance, records and training. Quality control is the practical testing within that programme: for example light beam alignment, tube output, kVp accuracy and AEC tests, done at set intervals (daily, monthly, quarterly, annually) to check performance and stability.

question: Describe the stages of QA through the life of an X-ray system. (4 marks)
model_answer: Acceptance testing checks that new equipment meets its specification and is safe before clinical use. Commissioning records baseline performance values. Routine performance testing compares later results with the baselines to detect and diagnose any deterioration. After a fault is corrected, testing verifies that the cause has been fixed. Maintenance continues throughout.
marking_points: Acceptance testing: meets specification, safe before use | Commissioning: baseline values recorded | Routine performance testing: detects change from baseline | Verification that faults have been corrected

question: Explain the IPEM Report 91 remedial and suspension levels, and what should happen at each. (4 marks)
model_answer: The remedial level is a level of performance at which action is needed, but the equipment may continue in use meanwhile. A risk assessment decides whether that is safe, a timescale for the fix is agreed and any restrictions are followed. The suspension level is a level of performance at which the equipment should be removed from clinical use immediately. Some subjective tests, such as image quality, have no suspension level. All results and actions are documented and followed up promptly.
marking_points: Remedial level: action needed, equipment may stay in use | Remedial: risk assessment, agreed timescale and restrictions | Suspension level: remove from clinical use immediately | Results documented and followed up promptly

question: Describe how the performance of an automatic exposure control is tested, and why it matters. (4 marks)
model_answer: Perspex or water phantoms of different thicknesses are exposed under AEC control at a range of tube voltages. The mAs and detector dose indicator are recorded; a working AEC gives a consistent detector dose for every combination. The chambers are compared with each other, and repeated exposures are checked for repeatability. The guard timer is tested by blocking the chambers with lead. This matters because a faulty AEC can over-expose patients, raising dose, or under-expose them, giving noisy images that may need repeating.
marking_points: Phantoms of different thicknesses at a range of kVp | Detector dose indicator and mAs recorded; should be consistent | Guard timer tested by blocking the chambers | A faulty AEC raises dose or gives poor images

learning_outcome: RDR-1173: radiation physics, protection and dosimetry
question: Explain why a QA programme is required in a radiography department. (4 marks)
model_answer: It is a legal requirement: IRR17 requires employers to provide a suitable QA programme so equipment keeps restricting exposure as far as reasonably practicable, and IR(ME)R 2017 also requires it. It is part of the HCPC standards of proficiency for radiographers. It keeps patient doses as low as reasonably practicable by detecting faults that raise dose. It keeps image quality consistent, avoiding repeats, missed diagnoses and wasted cost.
marking_points: Legal requirement under IRR17 and IR(ME)R 2017 | Part of the HCPC standards of proficiency | Keeps patient dose as low as reasonably practicable | Keeps image quality consistent, avoiding repeats and cost
